questions.question: Explain malnutrition
questions.solution_html:
• ( 5mks)
  • Definition of malnutrition
  • Classification
  • Symptoms and causative factors
  • Viscious cycle to be drawn for causative factors
  • Malnutrition refers to a condition resulting from an imbalance in nutrient intake, either insufficient or
  • excessive. This can be caused by a lack of essential nutrients (undernutrition), or by consuming too many
  • nutrients, potentially leading to obesity or related health issues (overnutrition). Malnutrition can manifest
  • in various forms, including wasting, stunting, and mental changes.
  • The most common types of malnutrition are Kwashiorkor , Marasmus and Marasmic Kwashiorkor.
  • Kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition, primarily affecting children, caused by a lack of protein in
  • the diet, despite sufficient calorie intake. It's characterized by edema (swelling), particularly in the
  • abdomen and extremities, along with other symptoms like skin changes, hair discoloration, and reduced
  • muscle mass. Cause
  • Kwashiorkor arises from a deficiency in protein, even when the individual has enough carbohydrates and
  • fats for energy.
  • Appearance
  • Affected individuals, especially children, may appear emaciated with a protruding abdomen due to fluid
  • retention (edema).
  • Symptoms
  • Edema: Swelling of the feet, ankles, and abdomen is a key indicator. Skin and Hair Changes: Skin may
  • become dry, scaly, and pigmented, and hair may lose its color and become brittle. Loss of Muscle Mass
  • Underweight individuals can have visible loss of muscle mass. Other Symptoms: Irritability, lethargy
  • and a weakened immune system are also common.
  • Consequences
  • Kwashiorkor can lead to severe health complications, including increased susceptibility to infections
  • growth retardation, and in severe cases, death, if not treated promptly.
  • Prevalence
  • It is most common in developing countries where access to protein-rich foods is limited, especially in
  • areas where the diet relies heavily on carbohydrates like rice or maize
  • Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition caused by a lack of calories and nutrients, leading to extreme
  • emaciation and a weakened body. It's characterized by a severe wasting of muscle and fat tissue, stunting
  • of growth, and a weakened immune system. The condition is often seen in young children, especially
  • those who are not properly fed or have diseases that interfere with nutrient absorption.
  • Aetiological factors
  • Repeated pregnancies, food fads and fallacies, frequent infections, improper sanitary practices, poverty
  • unclean drinking water, poor dietary knowledge
  • Key Characteristics of Marasmus
  • Severe Wasting
  • Individuals with marasmus appear extremely thin, with a noticeable loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat.
  • Stunted Growth:Children with marasmus experience significant delays in physical growth and
  • development. Weakened Immune System:Marasmus compromises the body's ability to fight off
  • infections, making individuals more susceptible to illnesses. Developmental Delays:The lack of essential
  • nutrients can also lead to cognitive and behavioral developmental delays in children.
  • Other Symptoms
  • These may include dry, brittle hair; sunken eyes; loose, wrinkled skin; and lethargy. Weight Loss
  • Marasmus is characterized by significant weight loss, often below 60% of the expected weight for age.
  • Causes
  • Marasmus can be caused by factors like inadequate feeding, physical defects preventing proper eating
  • diseases interfering with nutrient absorption, or infections causing loss of appetite.
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition that combines features of both marasmus and
  • kwashiorkor, resulting in a combination of wasting and edema. It's characterized by severe weight loss
  • muscle wasting, and fluid buildup in the body, particularly in the abdomen and extremities.
questions.final_answer: muscle wasting, and fluid buildup in the body, particularly in the abdomen and extremities

questions.question: Explain why pellagra is known 3D disease.
questions.solution_html:
• (2.5 mks ,2.5mks )
  • Pellagra is called the "3D disease" because it is characterized by three primary symptoms: dermatitis
  • dementia, and diarrhea. These symptoms arise from a deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3) in the diet.
  • Diarrhea (gastrointestinal mucositis)
  • Diarrhea occurs when the mucous lining of your intestines fails to replenish itself fast enough. Without
  • this mucosa, the intestines can’t digest properly, and they can’t protect themselves from irritation and
  • inflammation. Chronic inflammation affects the mucous lining along your entire gastrointestinal tract
  • from your mouth to bowels. This leads to gastrointestinal symptoms such as stomach pain and
  • indigestion, as well as symptoms of oral mucositis, which include mouth sores and a red, swollen tongue.
  • Dermatitis (skin photosensitivity)
  • Pellagra also produces a distinctive type of dermatitis, particularly on sun-exposed areas of the body, such
  • as the face, neck, arms, legs, hands and feet. Deprived of energy resources, the skin cells become more
  • photosensitive. Dermatitis begins with rashes that resemble a sunburn, then progresses to rough, scaly
  • hyper-pigmented plaques. One telltale feature is a dark, hyper-pigmented collar around the neck. It’s
  • called Casal’s collar, after the Spanish physician Don Gaspar Casal who first identified pellagra among
  • the Spanish peasants in 1735.
  • Dementia (brain and nerve damage)
  • Pellagra is a systemic disease, affecting the body as a whole as cells are deprived of the energy they need
  • to perform bodily functions. This will eventually affect the brain and nervous system. Early symptoms
  • may be vague. They may include lethargy, apathy, and difficulty concentrating, or they may look more
  • like anxiety or depression. Over time, symptoms progress to confusion and delusions. Severe cases may
  • lead to permanent dementia, as well as neurological damage resulting in balance and coordination
  • problems, muscle twitches and tremors.

questions.question: Describe how the deficiency of vitamin A and vitamin D affects the body.
questions.solution_html:
• ( 5mks)
  • Vitamin A deficiency happens when your body doesn’t get enough vitamin A. Diet lacking in vitamin A
  • and certain disorders can cause vitamin A deficiency. Symptoms include vision issues such as night
  • blindness. Treatment involves taking vitamin A supplements.
  • Vitamin A deficiency can lead to many complications, including
  • Eye problems: Vitamin A is a key factor in many functions of your eyes. Vision loss and blindness can
  • occur. One of the early signs of vitamin A deficiency is night blindness (nyctalopia). If you have night
  • blindness, you have trouble seeing well in the dark, but you can see normally if enough light is present. A
  • retinal disorder causes night blindness.
  • As the vitamin A deficiency worsens, the whites of your eyes and your corneas can become dry and you
  • aren’t able to produce tears (xerophthalmia). Foamy spots called Bitot spots may appear in the whites of
  • your eyes. Open sores on your corneas may appear, or drying or clouding of your corneas
  • (keratomalacia), which can lead to blindness.
  • Skin issues: A lack of vitamin A can cause dry, scaly and/or itchy skin.
  • Infertility: Vitamin A plays an important role in your reproductive system. Vitamin A deficiency can
  • lead to trouble conceiving and infertility.
  • Growth issues: Vitamin A deficiency can cause delayed growth and development in children.
  • Respiratory tract infections: Vitamin A deficiency can cause problems with your immune system. This
  • can lead to infections in your chest and throat.
  • Vitamin D
  • Vitamin D is an essential vitamin that your body uses for normal bone development and maintenance.
  • Vitamin D also plays a role in your nervous system, musculoskeletal system and immune system.
  • Severe lack of vitamin D in children causes rickets. Symptoms of rickets include
  • Incorrect growth patterns due to bowed or bent bones.,muscleweakness,bone pain, deformities in joints.
  • This is very rare. Children with a mild vitamin deficiency may just have weak, sore and/or painful
  • muscles.
  • Lack of vitamin D isn’t quite as obvious in adults. Signs and symptoms might include
  • Fatigue, bone pain.,muscle weakness, muscle aches or muscle cramps.,mood changes, like depression.
  • In general, the two main causes of vitamin D deficiency are
  • Not getting enough vitamin D in your diet and/or through sunlight.
  • Your body isn’t properly absorbing or using vitamin D.

questions.solution_html:
• Prevention and Management of protein deficiency disorders
  • (10mks)
  • Protein deficiency is when the intake is unable to meet body's requirements.Kwashiorkor and
  • marasmus are the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition recognized by
  • healthcare providers worldwide. The main difference between them is that kwashiorkor is
  • predominantly a protein deficiency, while marasmus is a deficiency of all macronutrients —
  • protein, carbohydrates and fats.
  • Kwashiorkor is a type of malnutrition characterized by severe protein deficiency. It causes fluid
  • retention and a swollen, distended abdomen. Kwashiorkor most commonly affects children
  • particularly in developing countries with high levels of poverty and food insecurity. People with
  • kwashiorkor may have food to eat, but not enough protein.
  • Kwashiorkor is one of the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition. People with
  • kwashiorkor are especially deficient in protein, as well as some key micronutrients. Severe
  • protein deficiency causes fluid retention in the tissues (edema), which distinguishes kwashiorkor
  • from other forms of malnutrition. People with kwashiorkor may look emaciated in their limbs
  • but swollen in their hands and feet, face and belly. The distended abdomen typical of
  • kwashiorkor can be misleading in people who are actually critically malnourished.
  • Kwashiorkor is rare in developed countries. It’s mostly found in developing countries with high
  • rates of poverty and food scarcity. Poor sanitary conditions and a high prevalence of infectious
  • diseases also help set the stage for malnutrition. Kwashiorkor can affect all ages, but it’s most
  • common in children, especially between the ages of 3 to 5. This is an age when many children
  • have recently transitioned from breastfeeding to a less adequate diet — one higher in
  • carbohydrates but lower in protein and other nutrients.
  • The difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus
  • Kwashiorkor and marasmus are the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition
  • recognized by healthcare providers worldwide. The main difference between them is that
  • kwashiorkor is predominantly a protein deficiency, while marasmus is a deficiency of all
  • macronutrients — protein, carbohydrates and fats. People with marasmus are deprived of
  • calories in general, either because they’re eating too little or expending too many, or both. People
  • with kwashiorkor may not be deprived of calories in general but are deprived of protein-rich
  • foods.
  • Symptoms and Causes
  • Edema (swelling with fluid, especially in the ankles and feet).
  • Bloated stomach with ascites (a build-up of fluid in the abdominal cavity).
  • Dry, brittle hair, hair loss and loss of pigment in hair.
  • Dermatitis — dry, peeling skin, scaly patches or red patches.
  • Enlarged liver, a symptom of fatty liver disease.
  • Depleted muscle mass but retained subcutaneous fat (under the skin).
  • Dehydration.
  • Loss of appetite (anorexia).
  • Irritability and fatigue.
  • Stunted growth in children.
  • Treatment
  • Marasmus
  • Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition characterized by a deficiency of all macronutrients
  • (proteins, carbohydrates, and fats), leading to a significant loss of body weight and tissue
  • particularly muscle and fat. It's primarily caused by a lack of sufficient calories and protein
  • intake, resulting in energy deficiency.
  • Causes
  • Inadequate calorie and protein intake: This can result from poverty, food shortages, or
  • inadequate breastfeeding.
  • Poor food choices: Limited access to diverse and nutritious foods can contribute to marasmus.
  • Increased energy expenditure: Conditions like chronic infections, burns, or other illnesses can
  • increase the body's energy needs, leading to marasmus if intake is not adequate.
  • Early weaning: Early weaning can result in inadequate feeding and starvation in infants.
  • Symptoms
  • Extreme weight loss: Body weight is significantly reduced, often below 62% of normal weight
  • for age.
  • Wasting: Muscle and fat tissue are depleted, leading to a thin, emaciated appearance.
  • Growth retardation: Children with marasmus may be stunted in size and development.
  • Irritability and lethargy: Lack of energy and reduced activity levels can be observed.
  • Changes in skin and hair: Skin may become dry and wrinkled, and hair can become thin and
  • brittle.
  • Other signs: Bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypotension (low blood pressure), and hypothermia
  • (low body temperature) can be seen.
  • Complications
  • Slow growth and development: Marasmus can lead to long-term growth and developmental
  • delays.
  • Increased susceptibility to infections: The weakened immune system makes individuals more
  • vulnerable to infections.
  • Serious complications: Diarrhea, measles, and respiratory infections can be life-threatening in
  • children with marasmus.
  • Treatment
  • Rehydration and electrolyte balance
  • Addressing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances is crucial.
  • Gradual refeeding
  • Providing a balanced diet, starting with small amounts and gradually increasing the volume and
  • nutritional content.
  • Addressing infections
  • Treating any underlying infections is essential to improve overall health and recovery.
  • Monitoring
  • Regular monitoring of weight, height, and other vital signs is needed to track progress and adjust
  • treatment as necessary.
  • Key differences from Kwashiorkor
  • Marasmus is a deficiency of all macronutrients (proteins, carbohydrates, and fats), while
  • kwashiorkor is primarily a protein deficiency.
  • Kwashiorkor often presents with edema (swelling) due to low protein levels, while marasmus is
  • characterized by muscle and fat wasting.
  • Marasmus is a serious condition that can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. Early
  • diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications and improve outcomes.
  • Marasmic Kwashiorkor
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition that combines features of both marasmus
  • and kwashiorkor. It occurs when a child with kwashiorkor (edematous malnutrition due to
  • protein deficiency) also experiences a significant calorie deficiency. The result is a condition
  • with both edema (swelling) and wasting (loss of muscle and fat mass).
  • Marasmic Kwashiorkor
  • A child with marasmus who also develops edema due to protein deficiency is classified as
  • marasmic kwashiorkor. This condition combines the wasting of marasmus with the edema of
  • kwashiorkor.
  • Causes
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor can develop when a child with kwashiorkor does not consume enough
  • calories, or when a child with marasmus experiences a sudden increase in protein deficiency.
  • Significance
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor is a serious condition with a high risk of complications and mortality, and
  • requires immediate medical attention.

questions.question: Write an essay on the signs and symptoms of protein deficiency. Elaborate / on Prevention and Management of protein deficiency dissorders

• Prevention and Management of protein deficiency disorders
  • (10mks)
  • Protein deficiency is when the intake is unable to meet body's requirements.Kwashiorkor and
  • marasmus are the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition recognized by
  • healthcare providers worldwide. The main difference between them is that kwashiorkor is
  • predominantly a protein deficiency, while marasmus is a deficiency of all macronutrients —
  • protein, carbohydrates and fats.
  • Kwashiorkor is a type of malnutrition characterized by severe protein deficiency. It causes fluid
  • retention and a swollen, distended abdomen. Kwashiorkor most commonly affects children
  • particularly in developing countries with high levels of poverty and food insecurity. People with
  • kwashiorkor may have food to eat, but not enough protein.
  • Kwashiorkor is one of the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition. People with
  • kwashiorkor are especially deficient in protein, as well as some key micronutrients. Severe
  • protein deficiency causes fluid retention in the tissues (edema), which distinguishes kwashiorkor
  • from other forms of malnutrition. People with kwashiorkor may look emaciated in their limbs
  • but swollen in their hands and feet, face and belly. The distended abdomen typical of
  • kwashiorkor can be misleading in people who are actually critically malnourished.
  • Kwashiorkor is rare in developed countries. It’s mostly found in developing countries with high
  • rates of poverty and food scarcity. Poor sanitary conditions and a high prevalence of infectious
  • diseases also help set the stage for malnutrition. Kwashiorkor can affect all ages, but it’s most
  • common in children, especially between the ages of 3 to 5. This is an age when many children
  • have recently transitioned from breastfeeding to a less adequate diet — one higher in
  • carbohydrates but lower in protein and other nutrients.
  • The difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus
  • Kwashiorkor and marasmus are the two main types of severe protein-energy undernutrition
  • recognized by healthcare providers worldwide. The main difference between them is that
  • kwashiorkor is predominantly a protein deficiency, while marasmus is a deficiency of all
  • macronutrients — protein, carbohydrates and fats. People with marasmus are deprived of
  • calories in general, either because they’re eating too little or expending too many, or both. People
  • with kwashiorkor may not be deprived of calories in general but are deprived of protein-rich
  • foods.
  • Symptoms and Causes
  • Edema (swelling with fluid, especially in the ankles and feet).
  • Bloated stomach with ascites (a build-up of fluid in the abdominal cavity).
  • Dry, brittle hair, hair loss and loss of pigment in hair.
  • Dermatitis — dry, peeling skin, scaly patches or red patches.
  • Enlarged liver, a symptom of fatty liver disease.
  • Depleted muscle mass but retained subcutaneous fat (under the skin).
  • Dehydration.
  • Loss of appetite (anorexia).
  • Irritability and fatigue.
  • Stunted growth in children.
  • Treatment
  • Marasmus
  • Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition characterized by a deficiency of all macronutrients
  • (proteins, carbohydrates, and fats), leading to a significant loss of body weight and tissue
  • particularly muscle and fat. It's primarily caused by a lack of sufficient calories and protein
  • intake, resulting in energy deficiency.
  • Causes
  • Inadequate calorie and protein intake: This can result from poverty, food shortages, or
  • inadequate breastfeeding.
  • Poor food choices: Limited access to diverse and nutritious foods can contribute to marasmus.
  • Increased energy expenditure: Conditions like chronic infections, burns, or other illnesses can
  • increase the body's energy needs, leading to marasmus if intake is not adequate.
  • Early weaning: Early weaning can result in inadequate feeding and starvation in infants.
  • Symptoms
  • Extreme weight loss: Body weight is significantly reduced, often below 62% of normal weight
  • for age.
  • Wasting: Muscle and fat tissue are depleted, leading to a thin, emaciated appearance.
  • Growth retardation: Children with marasmus may be stunted in size and development.
  • Irritability and lethargy: Lack of energy and reduced activity levels can be observed.
  • Changes in skin and hair: Skin may become dry and wrinkled, and hair can become thin and
  • brittle.
  • Other signs: Bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypotension (low blood pressure), and hypothermia
  • (low body temperature) can be seen.
  • Complications
  • Slow growth and development: Marasmus can lead to long-term growth and developmental
  • delays.
  • Increased susceptibility to infections: The weakened immune system makes individuals more
  • vulnerable to infections.
  • Serious complications: Diarrhea, measles, and respiratory infections can be life-threatening in
  • children with marasmus.
  • Treatment
  • Rehydration and electrolyte balance
  • Addressing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances is crucial.
  • Gradual refeeding
  • Providing a balanced diet, starting with small amounts and gradually increasing the volume and
  • nutritional content.
  • Addressing infections
  • Treating any underlying infections is essential to improve overall health and recovery.
  • Monitoring
  • Regular monitoring of weight, height, and other vital signs is needed to track progress and adjust
  • treatment as necessary.
  • Key differences from Kwashiorkor
  • Marasmus is a deficiency of all macronutrients (proteins, carbohydrates, and fats), while
  • kwashiorkor is primarily a protein deficiency.
  • Kwashiorkor often presents with edema (swelling) due to low protein levels, while marasmus is
  • characterized by muscle and fat wasting.
  • Marasmus is a serious condition that can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. Early
  • diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications and improve outcomes.
  • Marasmic Kwashiorkor
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition that combines features of both marasmus
  • and kwashiorkor. It occurs when a child with kwashiorkor (edematous malnutrition due to
  • protein deficiency) also experiences a significant calorie deficiency. The result is a condition
  • with both edema (swelling) and wasting (loss of muscle and fat mass).
  • Marasmic Kwashiorkor
  • A child with marasmus who also develops edema due to protein deficiency is classified as
  • marasmic kwashiorkor. This condition combines the wasting of marasmus with the edema of
  • kwashiorkor.
  • Causes
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor can develop when a child with kwashiorkor does not consume enough
  • calories, or when a child with marasmus experiences a sudden increase in protein deficiency.
  • Significance
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor is a serious condition with a high risk of complications and mortality, and
  • requires immediate medical attention.

questions.question: Explain about the mechanism of water balance.
questions.solution_html:
• (5mks, 5mks)
  • Water balance in nutrition refers to the equilibrium between water intake and water output in the
  • body. It's a crucial aspect of maintaining overall health and preventing dehydration or
  • overhydration. Water intake comes from fluids and the water content in food, while water output
  • occurs through urine, sweat, breathing, and faeces.
  • The body maintains water balance through a complex interplay of intake, output, and regulatory
  • mechanisms like ADH and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). These
  • mechanisms ensure that water levels in the body remain within a narrow, healthy range.
  • Fluid Intake
  • Thirst is a primary drive for fluid intake, stimulated by dehydration or increased sodium
  • concentration in the blood. The hypothalamus, particularly the osmoreceptors, plays a crucial
  • role in detecting these changes and triggering the thirst sensation.
  • Water Output
  • The kidneys are the primary organs for water excretion, adjusting urine concentration to reflect
  • the body's water needs. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, increases water
  • reabsorption in the kidneys, conserving water when the body is dehydrated.
  • Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
  • When blood volume decreases, the kidneys release renin, which activates the RAAS. This
  • system ultimately increases blood pressure and sodium reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to
  • increased water retention.
  • Kidney Function
  • The kidneys filter blood and produce urine, a process that helps regulate water and electrolyte
  • balance. They can adjust the amount of water reabsorbed back into the bloodstream based on the
  • body's needs.

questions.question: / Give the definitions for nutrition and health
questions.solution_html:
• Give the definitions for nutrition and health.
  • Nutrition
  •  Nutrition is the science of food, nutrients, and their effect on the body.
  •  It includes ingestion, digestion, absorption, utilization, and excretion of food.
  •  Proper nutrition is essential for growth, energy, repair, and maintenance of health.
  • Health
  •  Health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being.
  •  It is not merely the absence of disease.
  •  Good health enables an active and productive life
questions.final_answer:  Good health enables an active and productive life

questions.question: / Summarize the symptoms of iodine deficiency disorder (IDD)
questions.solution_html:
• Summarize the symptoms of iodine deficiency disorder(IDD).
  • Iodine deficiency affects thyroid hormone production and causes several disorders. Main
  • symptoms include
  •  Goitre – enlargement of thyroid gland causing neck swelling.
  •  Hypothyroidism – tiredness, weight gain, dry skin, slow metabolism.
  •  Weakness and fatigue.
  •  Poor concentration and low mental alertness.
  •  Growth retardation in children.
  •  Delayed puberty.
  •  Mental impairment in children.
  •  During pregnancy, severe deficiency may cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or cretinism
  • in babies

questions.question: / List the main food groups included in a plant-based diet.
questions.solution_html:
• List the main food groups included in a plant-based diet.
  • A plant-based diet mainly includes foods obtained from plant sources. Main food groups are
  •  Whole grains – rice, wheat, oats, maize, millet.
  •  Pulses and legumes – beans, peas, lentils, chickpeas, soybeans.
  •  Vegetables – leafy vegetables, roots, tubers, other vegetables.
  •  Fruits – banana, apple, orange, mango, berries etc.
  •  Nuts and seeds – almonds, walnuts, sesame, flaxseed, sunflower seeds.
  •  Plant oils – olive oil, coconut oil, groundnut oil.
  •  Herbs and spices for flavor and health benefits.
questions.final_answer:  Herbs and spices for flavor and health benefits

questions.question: / Elaborate on Polysaccharides
questions.solution_html:
• Elaborate on Polysaccharides.
  • Polysaccharides are complex carbohydrates composed of many monosaccharide units joined
  • together by glycosidic bonds. They usually contain more than ten sugar units and may consist
  • of hundreds or even thousands of glucose molecules. Polysaccharides are widely distributed
  • in plants, animals, and microorganisms. They are important in nutrition because they serve as
  • energy reserves, structural materials, and dietary fiber. Compared to simple sugars
  • polysaccharides are less sweet, less soluble, and digested more slowly.
  • Classification of Polysaccharides
  • Polysaccharides are mainly classified into homopolysaccharides and
  • heteropolysaccharides.

questions.question: / Explain the role of vitamin A in maintaining the overall health of a person.
questions.solution_html:
• Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for growth, vision, immunity, reproduction, and
  • maintenance of epithelial tissues. It occurs as retinol in animal foods and as beta-carotene in
  • plant foods. Vitamin A is required in small amounts but plays a major role in maintaining
  • overall health.
  • Sources of Vitamin A

  •  Liver
  •  Egg yolk
  •  Butter
  •  Milk
  •  Fish liver oils
  • Plant sources (carotene)
  •  Carrot
  •  Mango
  •  Papaya
  •  Pumpkin
  •  Spinach
  •  Green leafy vegetables

questions.question: / Explain the concept of climate-friendly nutrition and its importance in reducing environmental impact.
questions.solution_html:
• environmental impact.
  • Climate-friendly nutrition refers to dietary choices and food systems that promote human
  • health while reducing negative environmental effects such as greenhouse gas emissions
  • excessive water use, land degradation, and food waste. It focuses on selecting foods that are
  • nutritious, sustainable, and environmentally responsible.
  • Modern food production contributes significantly to climate change through methane
  • emission, deforestation, pollution, and waste generation. Climate-friendly nutrition aims to
  • create diets that protect both human health and the planet.
